name: Jamal Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Jamal, thanks for joining. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in policy and claims admin at an app-based insurer that sells travel and pet cover. Most of my day is the cases the app can't handle on its own: a vet bill in another language, a cancelled flight with a weird refund, a policy someone bought for the wrong dates. I use an AI assistant all day to summarise documents and draft replies, then I check and fix them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the person who builds the shortcuts. I wrote a set of prompts for reading foreign vet invoices that the whole team uses now. What wears me out is that the company's pitch is 'no humans needed', and I'm one of the humans, so every quarter feels like an audition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny, because I'd be a bit disappointed. I like the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say online that the tools are still useful even if they're not magic, and post a few of my prompt tricks. At work I'd say we should stop pretending the app runs itself. I'd probably be the one defending AI at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my job is pretty safe, because the app will always need someone for the strange cases. If AI stalls where it is, I'm the guy who knows its blind spots, and that's a very comfortable place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and push to formalise the prompt library into a real role, maybe 'automation lead' for the claims team. I'd keep investing a bit each month in an index fund, as I do now. I wouldn't change much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little disappointment. I'd have liked to see what these things could really do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said every quarter feels like an audition. Does that go away here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not fully. The company would still chase cost cuts, but my numbers are good and I'm the one who makes the tools work, so I'd feel fairly solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your colleagues who don't use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a guy, Arun, who refuses to touch them. In this world he's fine too, just slower. I'd keep nudging him, kindly.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful** even if they're not magic.
I'd tell colleagues to stop pretending the **app runs itself**.
think: My job is **safe** because strange cases still need a person.
Knowing the tools' **blind spots** makes me hard to replace.
do: Push to turn my prompt library into an **automation lead** role.
Keep investing monthly in an **index fund**.
feel: **Calm**, with mild **disappointment** at the tools stalling.
S0.quote: If AI stalls where it is, I'm the guy who knows its blind spots, and that's a very comfortable place to be.
fieldNote: Jamal is an **early adopter** who builds team shortcuts himself.
His company's **'no humans'** pitch keeps him on edge even here.
He'd nudge **non-users** gently rather than judge them.

steps.text: Pitch a formal automation lead role for the claims team
Keep paying into an index fund each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I think is already happening, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared: if a team of twelve does the work of twenty, give the twelve a four-day week, don't fire eight. I'd say it at work, and I'd write about it online. I'd also say people who get pushed out need real support, not a motivational video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the safer ones because I'm the one wiring it in. But I know I'm building the tools that will shrink my own team, and I don't feel great about being good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my manager in the first month and ask to lead the automation work officially, with a pay rise. I'd also start an online course in data and workflow design. And I'd try to get the tech workers' union a foothold, because nobody at an app company ever joins one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own spot looks fine, but my friends at work don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arun, and a woman named Lisa who handles complaints by phone. Lisa's brilliant with angry customers, but the app's chatbot is getting better at that every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lead the automation and also start a union. Is that awkward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. My manager would think I'm on both sides. I'd say I'm on the side of the work being done well and people being treated fairly, and that's not a contradiction.

I'd say pushed-out workers need **real support**, not videos.
think: I'm one of the **safer ones** because I build the automation.
I feel **uncomfortable** building tools that shrink my own team.
do: Ask my manager to lead **automation** officially, with a pay rise.
Start an online course in **workflow design**.
Try to bring the **tech workers' union** into the company.
feel: **Uneasy**: my job looks fine, but my **colleagues'** jobs don't.
S1.quote: I know I'm building the tools that will shrink my own team, and I don't feel great about being good at that.
fieldNote: Jamal holds an honest **conflict**: automating his team while organising it.
Progressive views push him toward **sharing gains** over cuts.
His security comes from being the one who **wires in the tools**.

steps.text: Ask his manager for an official automation lead role with a raise
Enrol in an online workflow design course
Invite the tech workers' union to meet staff at the insurer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one actually gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a political answer fast: a pause, a tax on the gains, a basic income while people adjust. I'd say it online and mean it. At work I'd say what everyone already knows, that a company selling 'no humans' will have no humans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my edge disappears. Being good with AI matters when AI needs a person to steer it, but full AGI doesn't. Being the best prompt writer in the office stops mattering the day the machine can write its own prompts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job while it lasts, max out my savings, and stop putting money into anything risky. I'd look hard at hands-on work, since that's three more years, maybe electrical work with my brother-in-law. And I'd get involved in campaigning for a basic income, properly, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got a cushion and I'm young, but the thing I'm good at would be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My girlfriend Mira works in marketing, so we'd both be in the first wave. I'd tell her we have about a year of runway between us and we should both pick a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your savings are strong. How long would they last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a year and a half if we're careful, and I've got some shares. That's real money, but it's not a plan if both of us are out.

say: I'd call for a **pause**, a tax on gains and a **basic income**.
I'd say a company selling **'no humans'** will end up with none.
think: My **AI skills** stop mattering once AI steers itself.
Both incomes at home are in the **first wave**.
do: Max out **savings** and pull money from risky investments.
Train in **electrical work** with my brother-in-law for the extra three years.
feel: **Anxious**: young and cushioned, but losing the **one skill** he's best at.
S2.quote: Being the best prompt writer in the office stops mattering the day the machine can write its own prompts.
fieldNote: Jamal's adaptability **stops protecting him** once AI needs no steering.
His girlfriend's **marketing job** doubles the household risk.
He moves from posting to **real campaigning**.

steps.text: Move investments into savings within the first three months
Start an electrical apprenticeship with his brother-in-law
Volunteer for a basic income campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Enough to see it coming and enough to be scared about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the next five years decide whether this goes well, so the rules need writing now. At work I'd push for a staff transition plan. Online I'd keep sharing what the tools can do, so people aren't blindsided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I get maybe three good years where my AI skills are worth extra, then it fades. That's useful time if I use it right. Five years is enough to get paid well for knowing AI, then use that money to learn a trade the machines reach last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the automation lead role and bank the higher pay. In year two or three I'd start an electrical course at night. And I'd keep pushing the union, because a transition plan only happens if someone asks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. The plan helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trips. Mira and I travel a lot, funny for someone selling travel cover. We'd do one a year instead of four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot delay matter much to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the whole plan. Electrical work lasts three years past the AGI date, and by then I'd hope there's some kind of support in place.

say: I'd say the **next five years** decide whether this goes well.
I'd keep showing people what the tools can do so nobody is **blindsided**.
think: My **AI skills** pay extra for maybe three years.
That money can fund a **trade** that machines reach last.
do: Take the **automation lead** role and bank the higher pay.
Start a night course in **electrical work** in year two or three.
Cut **travel** from four trips a year to one.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to get paid well for knowing AI, then use that money to learn a trade the machines reach last.
fieldNote: Jamal uses AI skills as a **bridge**, not a destination.
The **robot delay** is the backbone of his plan.
Cutting travel is a **concrete sacrifice** he names quickly.

steps.text: Take the automation lead role and save the pay rise
Start a night course in electrical work by year three
Cut holidays with Mira from four trips a year to one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's almost comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade to share the gains properly, and I'd be loud about the four-day week again. At work I'd say let's be the company that does it right. Online I'd be optimistic, which is rare for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I ride the wave for a long time. Ten years of being the person who makes AI useful is a career. Ten years of warning is a career, not a countdown, if I keep moving one step ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead automation at work, maybe move to a bigger insurer for more money in a couple of years. I'd invest more, maybe in a small flat. I'd also stay active in the union, because when the end comes, I want some rules in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but genuinely a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens around 2036 for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I'd be thirty-seven with money saved and a lot of experience in how these systems fail. Maybe I audit them for a regulator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move to a bigger insurer. Isn't that riskier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bigger insurers move slower, which here is a good thing. And plenty of them are hiring people like me nearby.

say: I'd push for a **four-day week** and shared gains over the decade.
I'd say our company could be the one that **does it right**.
think: Ten years of making AI useful is a **whole career**.
Staying **one step ahead** keeps the end from feeling like a countdown.
do: Lead **automation** at work, then move to a bigger insurer for more pay.
Stay active in the **union** to get rules in place.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is a career, not a countdown, if I keep moving one step ahead.
fieldNote: Long warning lets Jamal feel **optimistic**, unusual for him.
He imagines a later role **auditing AI** for a regulator.
Still keeps one foot in the **union** for the end game.

steps.text: Move to a larger insurer as automation lead within two years
Buy a small flat as an investment
Keep organising with the tech workers' union

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time for anyone to build rules or retrain. What would help is a basic income and paid training while people switch. I've spent years teaching the machine my job, and I'd like the people who own it to share some of what I taught it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask whether people like me feel guilty. I do, a bit, and I think lots of us do.

headlineQuote: I've spent years teaching the machine my job, and I'd like the people who own it to share some of what I taught it.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old** policy and claims clerk at an app-based travel and pet insurer.
He uses **AI tools daily** and wrote the prompt library his team relies on.
He's **progressive** and wants gains shared through a four-day week and unions.
He feels **guilty** building tools that may shrink his own team.
His plans run from **automation lead** to an electrical trade as AGI comes faster.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time for rules or retraining.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** and **paid training** while people switch work.
